query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An equiatomic, FCC-structured high-entropy alloy (e.g., the CoCrFeMnNi or 'Cantor' alloy) exhibits high ductility due to its favorable crystal structure that enables multiple slip systems and deformation mechanisms such as twinning and phase transformation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized equiatomic high-entropy alloy with an FCC-dominated microstructure.
generation.intervention: Utilize processing routes that stabilize the FCC phase (e.g., proper annealing or thermomechanical treatments) while limiting the formation of brittle intermetallics.
generation.conditions: Room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures where FCC slip and twin-assisted plasticity are active; standard ambient atmosphere without aggressive oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The inherent FCC lattice which provides numerous slip systems and may also foster deformation twinning.
generation.mechanism: The multiple slip systems available in the FCC structure, along with potential deformation twinning or mild phase transformation, accommodate plastic deformation. This results in an excellent strength–ductility trade-off where the lattice distortion from multiple principal elements further helps to redistribute strain and delay crack initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed FCC high-entropy alloy will exhibit enhanced ductility (improved uniform elongation and toughness) relative to alloys with primarily BCC phases, while still maintaining good strength.
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory or BCC-structured high-entropy alloys typically show brittleness; the substitution with an FCC-dominant phase composition improves ductility.
generation.boundary: The enhanced ductility is expected as long as processing does not trigger excessive formation of brittle intermetallic phases or secondary phases that could compromise the FCC matrix, and the temperature remains within a range that maintains FCC stability.
generation.uncertainty: While the FCC structure favors ductility, the precise balance of alloying elements, processing parameters, and microstructural stability may significantly affect the resulting mechanical properties. The exact ductility improvement is sensitive to these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens: one set processed to exhibit a predominantly FCC structure (e.g., via controlled annealing) and another set processed to develop a BCC-dominant microstructure. Conduct standardized tensile tests at room temperature and measure the elongation to failure and yield strength.
measurements: Microstructure characterization using XRD and electron microscopy to confirm phase composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FCC-dominant alloy does not show significantly higher ductility (e.g., more than a 20% increase in strain to failure) compared to the BCC-dominant alloy under identical testing conditions, or if additional deformation mechanisms (such as twinning) are not observed correlating with improved ductility, the hypothesis that the underlying FCC structure is the key mediator for ductility in these high-entropy alloys would be falsified.

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.
